idiom_name: #private field as an unforgeable brand + a non-exported constructor/factory
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no compile step and no copy operations to delete, so the realization combines two runtime properties: construction stays behind a factory (the class is not exported, or is only reachable through it) and each instance carries a `#private` field as an unforgeable brand. Private elements are managed by the engine as external metadata: they are invisible to property enumeration, are not carried by the prototype chain, cannot be created by spread/`Object.assign`, and the structured clone algorithm does not duplicate them - so a copy produced by `structuredClone` or a JSON round-trip loses the brand and throws a `TypeError` the first time a method touches it. Nothing here is a compile error, so the honest claim is 'copies cannot be made to work', not 'copies are rejected'; where the state is not a resource, prefer immutability. The classic base-class form has no analogue - the brand is the mixin.
pitfalls: The brand only protects instances that have it: an object literal, a subclass that does not run the constructor, or `Object.create(FileHandle.prototype)` fails the brand check - that failure is the guard, so never replace the private field with a public `fd` property.

`structuredClone`, spread and JSON round-trips silently produce a broken plain object with no private fields; the later method call throws an unhelpful TypeError, so wrap with a brand assertion if the failure mode matters.
`Object.freeze` stops mutation but not copying, and it has no effect on private elements - it is orthogonal to this pattern, not a substitute.
Because nothing is checked statically, the guarantee lives in code review; keep the constructor out of the module's exports and document the factory as the only entry point.
